title: FDA Authorizes First Robot for Autonomous Blood Draws, Clearing a Path for Clinical Deployment
excerpt: Vitestro's Aletta uses infrared imaging and ultrasound to find veins and draw blood without human hands, achieving a 94.5% first-stick success rate.
body:
• The FDA authorized Vitestro's Aletta on August 19 as the first standalone robotic device cleared for venous blood draws without direct human operation
  • The device uses near-infrared imaging and Doppler ultrasound to locate veins, achieving a 94.5% first-stick success rate in clinical trials
  • One phlebotomist can oversee three Aletta devices simultaneously, potentially tripling throughput in high-volume settings like hospitals and diagnostic labs
  • Vitestro has already received CE marking in Europe, where the device has been deployed in clinical settings for two years

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has authorized the first robotic device capable of drawing blood from patients without direct human assistance, a milestone that could reshape staffing models across hospitals, diagnostic laboratories, and blood donation centers grappling with a persistent shortage of trained phlebotomists.

How Aletta Works

Vitestro's Aletta, authorized on August 19 through the FDA's de novo regulatory pathway for novel medical devices, combines near-infrared imaging with Doppler ultrasound to map the patient's vein structure in real time. The system identifies the optimal puncture site, inserts the needle, draws the required blood volume, and processes the sample — all without a phlebotomist physically handling the needle.

In clinical trials, the device achieved a 94.5% first-stick success rate, a figure that compares favorably with human phlebotomists, whose first-attempt success rates in published studies typically range from 73% to 87% depending on patient demographics and vein accessibility. The device's performance advantage was most pronounced in patients with difficult venous access, including elderly patients, those with obesity, and individuals with a history of multiple failed blood draws.

"This isn't about replacing phlebotomists. It's about letting one skilled professional supervise three devices at once while maintaining quality that matches or exceeds manual draws."

— Vitestro CEO, on the staffing model for Aletta

Addressing a Workforce Crisis

The authorization arrives at a critical moment for the U.S. healthcare labor market. The American Society for Clinical Pathology has documented a chronic and worsening shortage of phlebotomists, with vacancy rates exceeding 20% at many hospitals and diagnostic networks. The shortage has contributed to longer patient wait times, delayed lab results, and increased reliance on costly traveling phlebotomists.

Vitestro's staffing model allows a single licensed phlebotomist to oversee three Aletta devices simultaneously, effectively tripling the throughput of one trained professional. This ratio was validated during the clinical trial phase and forms the basis of the company's commercial deployment strategy.

European Track Record

The U.S. authorization follows a two-year track record in Europe, where the device received CE marking and has been deployed in clinical settings across multiple countries. The company says the European deployment generated the real-world data that supported its FDA submission, including performance data across diverse patient populations.

Vitestro raised $70 million in a Series B round backed by a consortium that includes Labcorp, Mayo Clinic, and Sutter Health — strategic investors whose participation signals institutional confidence that the technology is ready for integration into large-scale clinical operations.

The Road to Clinical Adoption

The FDA cleared Aletta through the de novo pathway, a regulatory route reserved for novel devices that do not fit existing product classifications. The designation establishes a new regulatory category for autonomous venipuncture devices, creating a framework that future competitors will need to navigate.

Vitestro has not disclosed pricing for the device or a timeline for U.S. commercial availability. The company's investor lineup — anchored by some of the largest names in American laboratory medicine and hospital systems — suggests initial deployment is likely to target high-volume clinical environments where the phlebotomist shortage is most acute.

For patients, the practical promise is straightforward: fewer missed sticks, shorter waits, and more consistent sample quality. For health systems, the economic case rests on whether Aletta's capital and maintenance costs can undercut the fully loaded cost of human phlebotomists in a market where labor is both scarce and increasingly expensive.
